title: The cup, the blade and the treasure hall
hookLine: better to stop than to fill a cup to the brim; retire when the work is done (Tao Te Ching 9)
carry: when the work is done, step back
last: THE HIGHEST GOOD HELPS ALL AND TAKES THE LOW PLACE.

cards: A mug of coffee, poured right to the rim, carried from the counter to the couch. Every step is a negotiation: eyes locked on the surface, tiny shuffling steps.
A little slops over anyway, onto the hand, onto the rug, and the whole walk is spent guarding the cup instead of enjoying it. One more splash from the pot did all that.
Leave a finger's width at the top and the walk is easy. Chapter nine of the Tao Te Ching opens with a full vessel of its own, then gives three more pictures like it.

teach.h: THE CUP: NOT TO THE BRIM.
teach.b: First, the cup. Legge's translation begins: "It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full." Not empty; just not full to the brim.
The last bit of filling is what makes the carrying hard.
Second, the blade. Keep sharpening an edge, the chapter says, and it won't keep its sharpness for long; past a point, more work only wears it away. Third, the hall of treasure.

teach.h: THE HALL: TOO MUCH TO GUARD.
teach.b: Fill a hall with gold and jade, and no one can guard it all; when wealth and honor make someone proud, they bring harm on themselves.
A cup, a blade, a treasure hall, a proud name: each something good, pushed one step too far. The chapter isn't against coffee, or sharp knives, or wealth. It's about the extra splash.
The chapter's last line, in Legge's words: "When the work is done, and one's name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven." Seasons do this.
Summer doesn't stay on to be admired; it does its work and steps back, and autumn comes. Stopping, here, isn't failure or quitting. It's knowing when the work is done.

how: Some readers use chapter nine as a check on overwork and excess, choosing to stop a task when it is done well enough rather than polishing or adding past that point.

games.q: what does “stop before it spills” mean?
o: clean up a mess before anyone sees it
quit while there's still room at the top
never start anything you can't finish

games.q: the project is finished and it's good. people are starting to praise you for it. what does chapter nine say to do?
o: keep polishing it so the praise keeps coming.
step back: the work is done.
start a bigger project right away to top it.
games.why: "When the work is done, and one's name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven."

practice: Look over today and tomorrow for the place you're about to pour one more splash: one more email tonight, one more episode, one more edit to something already finished.

Picture yourself stopping a little short of the rim, and notice what it's like to carry the cup with room at the top. If you pray, you can ask for help stopping; if not, breathe with the room you've left.

wordCard.voice: Stop before it spills. Chapter nine's cup, blade, treasure hall and proud name, and its last line: when the work is done, step back. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, gōng suì shēn tuì: the work done, the self withdraws. From the close of Tao Te Ching 9.

carryVoice: Your line: when the work is done, step back. A week of chapters ends here: no contest, the knot untied, the valley, the one who goes last, water in the low place, and now a cup with room at the top. I'll be here tomorrow.
